meta.chapterLabel: Lesson 1: Meeting: Nice to Meet You

items.note: Marks belonging/affiliation between two nouns, ordered [owner] の [thing]: see のぞみデパートのたなかさん (Nozomi Depaato no Tanaka-san), '(the) Tanaka-san of Nozomi Department Store,' in this lesson's introduction sentence.
Suffix — attaches after a person's name; cannot be used after one's own name
items.hint: the polite title placed after a name

items.note: Suffix — attaches directly after a noun with no space to state what someone or something is; means 'is/am/are'. Example: (わたしは (watashi wa)) スミスです (sumisu desu)。 — '[I am] Smith.'

Added to the very end of a です (desu) sentence to turn it into a yes/no question, with no change to word order, e.g. アメリカじんですか (amerikajin desu ka), 'Is (he) American?' — unlike English, you don't invert word order or add a helper word.
A plain 'yes,' confirming a yes/no question; compare そうです (sou desu), which affirms a specific statement outright rather than just answering yes.
Confirms or affirms a statement outright ('that's right') — a direct answer, not just an acknowledgment of what you heard.
Said once, at the very first meeting with someone — never again after that. Typically followed by stating your name + です (desu), then よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu).

items.english: I look forward to working with you.
items.target: よろしくおねがいします
items.note: Said right after introducing yourself, usually preceded by はじめまして (hajimemashite) and your name + です (desu); the person you're greeting replies with こちらこそ (kochirakoso), 'likewise.' Here おねがいします is fused into a set greeting idiom, not the standalone request use seen in もういちどおねがいします (mou ichido onegaishimasu, 'once more, please') from the earlier lesson.
A polite reply to よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), meaning 'likewise' / 'the pleasure is mine' — said back after the other person says it to you.

Follows noun 1, marking it as the sentence topic; similar to 'as for' in English. Example: スミスさんは (sumisu-san wa) アメリカじんです (amerika jin desu)。 — 'As for Smith-san, (he) is American.' (i.e. 'Smith-san is American.')
Polite way to say 'this person' when introducing someone, as in こちらは…です (kochira wa … desu), 'this is …'.
Used freely regardless of politeness level. Contrast あなた (anata, 'you'), which is used far less than English 'you' — addressing someone by name + さん (san) is usually preferred instead.
A plain 'no', answering a yes/no question. The same word is also used to politely wave off thanks or praise — see いいえ used for 'Not at all'.
じん (jin) attaches to a country name to mean 'a person of that country' — the same pattern gives イギリスじん (igirisujin), ドイツじん (doitsujin), ちゅうごくじん (chuugokujin), and more.

items.target: たなかさんはにほんじんです
items.reviewNote: Added as a dedicated example of the topic-marker は — mirrors this chapter's own Key Sentence 1 pattern (Name + は + nationality + です), using different vocabulary already in this lesson

items.target: スミスさんはアメリカじんです
スミスさんはアメリカじんですか
はい、アメリカじんです
いいえ、イギリスじんです

items.english: This is Tanaka-san of the Nozomi Department Store.
items.target: こちらはのぞみデパートのたなかさんです
items.note: こちらは (kochira wa) introduces someone, and のぞみデパートの (Nozomi Depaato no) shows affiliation with の (no), following the [company] の [person] pattern.
Direct 'you' is used far less in Japanese than in English — addressing someone by name + さん (san) is usually more natural and polite than あなた (anata).
Plain word for 'country.' Add the honorific prefix お (o) and it becomes おくに (okuni), 'your country' — see that card and お (o) itself — used to ask about someone else's home country, never your own.

Prefix — attaches before a noun as an honorific. Example, from this chapter's own Target Dialogue: スミスさん (sumisu-san)、おくには (o-kuni wa) どちらですか (dochira desu ka)。 — 'Smith-san, what country are you from?' (お (o) + くに (kuni) = 'your country'.)
items.hint: the prefix on native words like なまえ (namae) and みやげ (miyage)

items.note: お (o) + くに (kuni, 'country') — the honorific prefix makes this specifically 'your country' (or a third person's), never your own. Heard in おくにはどちらですか (okuni wa dochira desu ka), 'What country are you from?'
Polite word for 'where,' used here to ask about someone's home country: おくにはどちらですか (okuni wa dochira desu ka), 'What country are you from?'

items.english: Smith-san, what country are you from?
items.target: スミスさん、おくにはどちらですか
items.reviewNote: Drawn directly from this chapter's own Target Dialogue
items.note: Demonstrates the honorific お (o) attaching to くに (kuni) ('country') to form おくに (okuni) ('your country')

items.target: たなかさんをおねがいします
items.reviewNote: Placeholder filled with 'たなかさん', the exact example given in the chapter's own NOTES section (source shows only '〜を おねがいします')
items.note: Here おねがいします (onegaishimasu) follows a person's name + を (o) to ask a receptionist to call them over, e.g. たなかさんをおねがいします (Tanaka-san o onegaishimasu); contrast もういちどおねがいします (mou ichido onegaishimasu) from the earlier lesson, where おねがいします stands alone after the request word instead.
